ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Maxillofacial Prosthodontics Referral — Sigmund Freud — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Establishing primary care seven years after maxillectomy for palatal cancer: about twenty cigars a day, a worn obturator, pain and weight loss

text.paragraph: Worn obturator seven years after a right partial maxillectomy for palatal squamous cell carcinoma, with pain where it rubs, hypernasal speech, nasal leakage of liquids and weight loss, in a 74-year-old man who smokes about twenty cigars a day. Please assess and treat the prosthesis and advise on speech, swallowing and dental care. [S]
Urgency: Within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Can the obturator be relined or adjusted now, and does he need a new one?
Is the sore area at the defect margin caused by the prosthesis, or does anything need a biopsy or his surgeon's review?
What can be done for his speech and the nasal leakage of liquids?
What dental and prosthesis care do you advise for his remaining teeth and the defect?
Which form of nicotine replacement works best with an obturator, and how does smoking affect the prosthesis and the tissues?

text.paragraph: Squamous cell carcinoma of the right hard and soft palate seven years ago, treated by right partial maxillectomy with clear margins (pT2 N0) and no radiation; definitive obturator made at the time and never replaced; yearly surveillance by his head and neck surgeon with no recurrence, last examination ten months ago. About twenty cigars a day for about fifty years. Pain 6 of 10 at the defect margin and right cheek; liquids leak into his nose; speech hypernasal; weight down 4 kg in six months to 58.4 kg, albumin 3.4 g/dL, hemoglobin 13.2 g/dL. No allergies. Started today: varenicline (before a quit date), scheduled acetaminophen 1,000 mg three times daily, a soft high-protein diet with supplements [S]

list.item: He doubts he can work without cigars and has failed to stop many times. [S]
His obturator leaks and rubs, which makes speaking, eating and working harder. [S]
He fears the cancer coming back. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Sigmund Freud was born Sigismund Schlomo Freud on May 6, 1856, in Freiberg, Moravia, now in the Czech Republic; in 1860 his family settled in Vienna. [D]
In the 1880s he experimented with cocaine himself, praised it in his paper On Coca (1884), and urged others to use it before he realized it could be addictive. [D]
According to his personal physician's account, as summarized in a 2019 review, he still used cocaine regularly in the 1890s. [D]

He began smoking in his twenties, first cigarettes and then cigars, following the example of his father, and often smoked about twenty cigars a day; his biographer described it as an addiction rather than a habit. [D]

In 1894, at 38, his friend the physician Wilhelm Fliess attributed his irregular heartbeat to smoking and told him to stop. He tried repeatedly and failed: one attempt ended within seven weeks, and a later one lasted fourteen months before he started again, describing the abstinence as torture. [D]
In 1923, at 67, he was diagnosed with cancer of the right upper jaw and palate, a squamous cell carcinoma; a first excision in April 1923 was followed by radiation treatment. [D]

Later in 1923 the oral surgeon Hans Pichler performed a radical operation that removed part of the upper jaw and soft palate, and made the obturator prosthesis that closed the defect; Freud called it "the monster." Pichler provided most of his later prosthetic care. [D]
He kept smoking cigars after the cancer was diagnosed and refused to give them up. [D]
At 73, after a heart illness, he stopped smoking for 23 days and then gradually started again. [D]

list.item: Tobacco use disorder, severe: about twenty cigars a day for about fifty years, with many failed attempts to stop; synthetic modern episode linked to his documented cigar smoking: active, confirmed [S]

Squamous cell carcinoma of the right hard and soft palate seven years ago, treated by right partial maxillectomy with clear margins (pT2 N0) and no radiation in this synthetic history, with no recurrence on yearly surveillance: active, confirmed [S]
Acquired defect of the right maxilla and palate after maxillectomy, closed with an obturator prosthesis that is now worn and fits poorly: active, confirmed [S]
Hypernasal speech and nasal leakage of liquids from a poorly sealing obturator: active, confirmed [S]
Chronic pain at the maxillectomy site and right cheek, worse where the obturator rubs: active, confirmed [S]
Raised LDL cholesterol (126 mg/dL) with a high estimated 10-year cardiovascular risk after fifty years of smoking: active, confirmed [S]
Weight loss of 4 kg in six months from painful chewing and leakage, with a low albumin: active, confirmed [S]

Tobacco: a nonjudgmental assessment of readiness and of what cigars do for him; varenicline started now, before a quit date, with a plan to cut down and then stop; combination nicotine replacement (patch and lozenge) added from the quit date; cigars are counted like any other tobacco; weekly behavioral support by phone with the national quitline and in clinic; relapse treated as part of the process. Guideline: Initiating Pharmacologic Treatment in Tobacco-Dependent Adults. An Official American Thoracic Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2020); Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

Head and neck cancer survivorship: yearly examination of the mouth, defect and neck by his head and neck surgeon (more than five years after treatment), self-examination of the mouth, prompt review of any sore, lump, bleeding or change that lasts two weeks, imaging only for symptoms, and counseling on the risk of second primary cancers of the mouth, throat, larynx, esophagus and lung, which stopping smoking lowers. Guideline: NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology: Head and Neck Cancers, Version 2.2026 (follow-up and survivorship) (2026); American Cancer Society Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Care Guideline (2016) [S]

Chronic pain: scheduled acetaminophen up to 3,000 mg a day, a well-fitting obturator, warm saline rinses, and no long-term opioids; the plan is reviewed at each visit with a pain score. Guideline: American Cancer Society Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Care Guideline (2016); CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain — United States, 2022 (2022) [S]

Nutrition: dietitian advice on soft high-protein meals, oral nutrition supplements twice daily, weight at each visit and albumin rechecked. Guideline: American Cancer Society Head and Neck Cancer Survivorship Care Guideline (2016) [S]

Cardiovascular risk: lipid panel and 10-year risk estimate; a statin discussed with him once the smoking plan is under way. Guideline: Statin Use for the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease in Adults: Preventive Medication (2022) [S]
Referral to maxillofacial prosthodontics, Clara Vasquez-Lindqvist, DDS, ordered 1930-06-01 [S]
